passage: I was at the next table at the college farewell dinner, so I saw most of it. Nilesh had been drinking since the start. By eleven he was slurring, knocking over glasses, and when a waiter asked him to sit, he got loud and shoved a chair. Then, suddenly, he went very sleepy, head on the table. When he didn't answer properly, she turned him on his side on the bench and told me to call an ambulance. I did. The paramedics said she'd done the right thing.

passage: Farida, you're going to college parties now, so let your Naveen Mama tell you one story. When I was twenty, at a friend's birthday in Hyderabad, my friend Sunil drank far too much. At first he was loud, then he started picking fights. Then, near midnight, he slumped down in the corner and wouldn't wake up properly. Everyone laughed and said let him sleep it off. I didn't like the look of him. His breathing was strange. So I stayed. I turned him on his side, the way our first-aid teacher had shown us, and told my friend to call an ambulance. The doctors said later it was a good thing we did. Sunil and I are still friends. So promise me: if a friend can't be woken, don't laugh, don't leave. Stay and get help.

passage: In the village near Muzaffarpur, Ganga, nineteen, ran a small tailoring stall from the front of the house. Her elder brother Kiran had started drinking country liquor with the other men in the evenings. Now it was most nights. He came home loud, slept past noon and asked her for money. At the well, the women whispered, and Ganga walked home with her face burning. She lay awake worrying he'd hurt himself on the road, then felt furious at him in the morning. She was exhausted. One day she went to the women's self-help group and told them. They listened. The leader said, 'You can't stop him. But you can stop paying for it, and you can look after yourself.' That evening, when Kiran asked for money, Ganga said, 'No. I love you, but no.'
